utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, can you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. It's IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. I would like to greet all people present in the courtroom, the representatives from the Prosecution, Defence counsel, and the accused. An oral decision which amends a written decision, 16th of October, 2006. We handed down a written decision on the evidence presented through Peter Hauenstein, the document P 3273, which had been presented by the Defence of Mr. Coric. This document is still admitted, but it's a document that has been admitted now under seal, because it's a document that complies pursuant to Article 70 -- to Rule 70. The Prosecution still has a short time to go, and I shall give them the floor straight away. I would also like to greet the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Williams.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Mr. Williams, yesterday evening when we left the court, you were talking about Colonel Siljeg and General Petkovic and their relationship. You told the Court that, according to the information that you had obtained in the field, that Colonel Siljeg was the head of the operational zone north-west Herzegovina and that his superior was Brigadier Petkovic, who was the commander of the HVO. This is on transcript page 8518 of yesterday's transcript. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, I see you still have your exhibit bundle there. Could you please look at Exhibit 1153. Mr. Williams, have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have. I saw it on Sunday.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: What's the date of the document?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the 15th of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And who is the author of the document?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Brigadier Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Focusing your attention on the first paragraph of the document, is it fair to say that this document confirms what you said yesterday about the relationship between General Petkovic and Colonel Siljeg?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Could you then move to Exhibit 1292, please. Have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I saw it on Sunday.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Who's the author of the document?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Brigadier Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And to whom is the document addressed?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the commander of the Mostar south-eastern Herzegovina zone of operations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, thank you. I only wish to draw attention to the signature on this document, not the typewritten name of the signatory but the signature itself. I suggest that this signature be compared to other signatures by General Milivoj Petkovic for the following reasons: On the 24th of January, Milivoj Petkovic was attending negotiations in Geneva so he did not sign this document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. But this signature is on behalf of Mr. Petkovic, for Mr. Petkovic. The question which remains is to know whether it's a head of staff, a second in command, an officer. We'll have to see that later.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, could you just briefly just read the order and tell us what the order is about?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a troop rotation order, reinforcement order, to send troops from other units to relieve troops that are in position around Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And where do these new troops come from?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ljubuski, Grude, Siroki Brijeg, and Citluk.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Let me now focus your attention to Exhibit 1311, which is in the second bundle. Have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have, on Sunday.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Again, who is the author of the document? Page 9.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Siljeg.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And going back to the first page, what's the date of the document?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 26th of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And to whom is the document addressed?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Presidency of the HVO of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, government of the HVO HZ HB in Mostar, the defence department in Mostar, and the Main Staff of the HVO in Mostar, and to his own operation zone in Tomislavgrad.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, there's just two small things that I want to point out in this particular order. If you move to page 2 of the order, in the top paragraph, line 5, and I'll read it out, it says the following: "Carried out talk with Andabak on Brada's orders." And then if you move to page number 8, somewhere in the middle, second paragraph, bottom of the paragraph of the second paragraph, it says: "While writing the report, I was informed of the instructions which Zrinko Tokic obtained from Brada and I shall follow them." Now, Witness, do you know who Brada is?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did used to know who Brada is. I cannot be specific or exactly recall who Brada is now.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: So you're saying here that you recall the name Brada when you were in Gornji Vakuf. You recall that this name came up.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: But you can't remember who Brada is?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It's somebody of a higher rank than Colonel Siljeg.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you. Moving to another topic, Witness, can you say something about the general manner in which the HVO attacked the area of Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I'm sorry. There's just one thing I'd like to look at. I've got a document here, and I notice a few things at times on this document. On page 7 in the English version, Witness, it is mentioned that the participation and involvement of UNPROFOR is considered at each check-point. That said, the check-point -- these check-points will be manned by mixed patrols. As far as you remember, did you ever happen to be there at the check-point when the HVO and ABiH were there together?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were occasions at the start of cease-fires where they would work together, and they even had representatives from each of the side on the other side's mortar positions, such as to verify that they weren't firing. However, it was sporadic, and it depended a lot on the immediate situation, though sometimes we would go to collect the people for these joint patrols and one side or the other would not join in. But, yes, there were occasions when they did jointly patrol.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. But my question concerned UNPROFOR. Why, for instance, did the BritBat not put some of its men at these check-points at the same time as the HVO and ABiH? Because this proposal had been put forward by Colonel Siljeg. What I wanted to know is why BritBat did not take part in this kind of control. According to me, this would have been beneficial in that you could have controlled people going in, going out, and I would like to know why UNPROFOR did not take part, together with the other two entities, did not take part in controlling the roads.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I understand now, Your Honour. Yes, we did actually take part in the joint patrols. In three specific areas, we had had a check-point on each of the routes going into Gornji Vakuf where we had a Warrior, infantry fighting vehicle, with a section of troops and a representative from each of the two factions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So at the entrance of Gornji Vakuf you'd placed a tank at the spot where the two warring factions were, the two warring parties.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were three check-points; one on the southern edge of Gornji Vakuf, one on the northern edge of Gornji Vakuf, and one just up the road from our base. They were primarily there to reassure the two factions and also to reassure the locals and also to keep the routes open so we could keep the aid moving through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. You have answered my questions. Mr. Bos, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, at the time you were there in Gornji Vakuf, did you ever see how the HVO would attack areas in Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The main method, when they were attacking the villages around Gornji Vakuf, was to use mortars, heavy machine-guns and artillery and tank fire to either get the civilian population in the village to leave, in which case then the militia that -- the Muslim militia that were there would leave because there would be nobody to protect; or the other way around, to get the Muslim militia to leave, in which case the Muslim population would leave because there was nobody to protect them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And when you say that they were using mortars and artillery to attack, would they actually, as far as you could tell, aim at military targets?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was very random. They would just aim at a village or aim at an area in the town and just fire into it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are answering a question that has been put to you by the Prosecution. This has bothered me all night. Yesterday, we saw a document which discussed the military police. The military police had 10 people killed and over 60 people wounded, so all in all, there were 80 casualties amongst the military police. These were the people that suffered in combat, out of 430. In other words, 20 per cent of all these men were lost. You're talking about artillery fire and you're -- the attack. This what happens in modern attacks. You start using your weaponry and then the men are on the ground. How can you explain this? Twenty per cent of the people working for the military police were either wounded or killed. Does this mean that around Gornji Vakuf or in Gornji Vakuf there were pockets there that remained, and the infantry was confronted with a certain amount of resistance? How can you explain this? If there are artillery shells falling, how come the HVO suffered so many casualties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The chosen method of using heavy weaponry to try to get them to move out didn't work. In most of the villages, the people stayed, so that necessitated them having to be cleared on foot, which is -- urban warfare, even in a small village, heavily favours the defender, and you would expect to take heavy casualties. Most commanders will try, at all cost, to avoid engaging an enemy inside a built-up area solely because of that -- the heavy casualty rate and also the heavy expenditure of small-arms ammunition that clearing buildings uses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for your answer, which is helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, could you look at Exhibit 1235, please. Looking at the first page, what kind of document is this?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a Cheshire Regiment military information summary for the 20th of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to focus your attention on page 3, and in particular the top paragraph, and could you please read out the sentence which starts with "In addition ..."

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: "In addition, a great deal of HVO artillery fire has proved ineffective, falling mainly on Muslim residential areas and not close to the main concentrations of Muslim fighters. In short, the HVO have met with only partial success and have not managed to break into the town itself."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, is this exactly as you just testified, when you said that HVO would fire artillery into villages without actually aiming at military targets?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Artillery and mortars are not a point weapons; they're an indirect area-fire weapon. You shell an area as opposed to a specific target.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, could you also look at Exhibit 1278. What kind of document is this?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a Cheshire Regiment military information summary. It says its dated the 23rd of November on that line and the 23rd of January on the line above it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: So, what would you think? Would this be a document of the 23rd of November or 23rd of January? Just --

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 23rd of January.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Very well. Going to page 2 of this document, under the heading "Gornji Vakuf," and I'll read out the part which I'm particularly interested in. It's a bit after the middle of the paragraph. "The village of Bistrica, grid 0770, came under rocket attack from an HVO BM21. The houses in the village were reported to be burning fiercely. CO 1 Cheshire is keen to stress that this is most definitely ethnic cleansing by Croats on a Muslim village." Witness, did you actually, yourself, witness this particular attack on Bistrica?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Bistrica was small village to the rear of our base, approximately 400 yards away from the base. We saw the first Salvo of rockets land on the hill in the woods behind the village, and then a second Salvo was fired which landed on the village itself. It caused a significant amount of damage. Most of the village was damaged, on fire. There were bodies in the streets, and at one stage we had to go and shoot the dogs because the dogs were eating the bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And the village of Bistrica, is it a Muslim village or a Croat village?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a mixed village, but they live on separate sides of the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: In which part of the village was it?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The majority of munitions fell onto the Muslim side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, following on what you've just said, I would like to understand. A while ago you said that the HVO had suffered casualties because the artillery had not defeated the combatting forces, and the HVO, therefore, entered the village which caused casualties on both sides. What I would like to know is this: When the HVO shelled a village, where were the ABiH fighters? Were they inside the village, inside the houses, in trenches, outside the village? Where are these people? Because after the shelling, when the HVO then enters the village and there is fighting in the village, where were the ABiH men at the time the shells and mortars were falling?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Most of the villages were defended by TO, which are a militia of -- not as high quality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. They were defended by the Territorial Defence. The members of the Territorial Defence, where were these people in the village? Where were they, inside the houses, outside the houses, in holes they had dug themselves, in cellars? Where were these people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were in all of those, Your Honour, as they'd constructed bunkers, fire trenches. Some of them were in their houses because they were their houses, they lived there. So they were all over the place within the village area itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, let's take an 82-millimetre mortar, which is in its right position, and a shell falls on the village. Who does the HVO aim at, the houses, the people inside the houses, the civilians, the members of the Territorial Defence? Who is targeted by the shell that's about to fall on the house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The village itself, Your Honour. With a mortar you cannot fire at a specific point target. My profession in the British Army was as a senior mortar fire controller. A mortar has a beaten zone and a very, very good mortar team, who are well practised with up-to-date equipment, can get a mortar round to land within 40 metres of what they're trying to hit. That's why they tend -- when you see a mortar firing, they fire an awful lot of ammunition. It's to create a beaten area. Mortars against any -- particularly medium mortars, like 82-millimetre mortars, are not a very good weapon for using against well-dug-in troops as they don't contain a lost explosive. They're mainly a shrapnel weapon. And all you will succeed, in using them against soldiers, is to slow them down, make them go to cover. But you'll be very hard pushed to damage a constructed defence with a medium-calibre mortar. Houses, they will -- depending on how the fuse is set, as you can have a delayed fuse or an impact fuse, houses are not that much protection, really, unless you're in a cellar, or something like that, as a round may come through the roof and explode inside the building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for having given me these technical details.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, could you please look at Exhibit 1406. Could you tell us what kind of document this is?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a Cheshire Regiment military information summary from the 3rd of February, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Could I focus your attention to page 3 of this document. Now, as you can see on this page, there are casualty figures listed. Reading this report, were these casualty figures that you reported in this report?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And are these casualty figures from Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And could you please read out here in court -- well, let me first ask you: How did you obtain these casualty figures?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We got them from the commanders of both sides while they were in talks.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And could you please read out the figures that have been reported here, and maybe let's start with -- because the report makes a division between military and civilian casualties and -- dead, so let's start with the military dead.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: On line 1, the HVO Croatian: Military dead, 40; civilian dead, nil. For the armija and the Muslims: Military dead, 21; civilian dead 39. On the third line, for the HVO and Croats: Military wounded, 79; civilian wounded, not known. For the armija and Muslim side, a total of 200 military and civilian wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, finally, I would like you to look at Exhibit 1437. Have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I saw it on Sunday.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Who's the author of the document?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Brigadier General Milivoj Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Moving back to the front page, what's the date of the document?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the 8th of February, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And what kind of document is this?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a situation report of what's going on at that particular moment in time in Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, I would like to focus your attention on page 2 of this document, and I'm interested in the middle paragraph, which says, "Report from Prozor." Could you please read out the sentence that starts with "Both sides ..." up to the end of the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Both sides are still taking prisoners, including women and children. Prisoners are being exchanged. The talks are continuing but the agreements are not being observed. Cease-fire orders have been reissued. Our side has continued to burn down buildings - Uzricje, Zdrimci, Dusa, Krupa. Both sides are retaliating in wilful acts of individuals. There are also cases of mutilation."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, what's been reported here in this report from Petkovic, is that what you experienced on the ground as well around this time?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: May I just ask, when you speak of mutilation here, what do you refer to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The mutilation of corpses, Your Honour. I personally only saw one incident, and that was where some Croat civilians had been killed, and then after they'd been killed, barbed wire had been wrapped around their throats.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, for the transcript, with respect to this document in B/C/S, number 1437, it says that it was not signed by General Petkovic, there is no signature; whereas I note that there isn't a register number here. Usually all military documents have a number. Here, we don't see a number. But the date is there, the 8th of February, 1993. Having said that, continue, Mr. Bos.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, do you recall whether the ABiH and the HVO, in one of their cease-fire negotiations, decided to set up a joint commission?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And can you explain the role of this joint commission? What did it do?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The joint commission would be a member from each of the two factions and a member from UNPROFOR, and they would go and visit outlying areas and villages and catalogue the damage and the casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: When was this joint commission set up?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the end, when we had a stable cease-fire. I can't remember the exact date, but it was at the end of the fighting. It was part of the actual cease-fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And did you participate in any of these joint commissions?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did participate in two or three.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And you said that they visited villages. How many villages were visited in total; do you recall?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every village in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And how long did it take this joint commission to visit these villages?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was several days.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And so you said that you joined in one of these joint commissions. What was your role when you would actually visit the village? Could you explain a little bit how this would go in practice?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our role was to basically make sure that the two representatives from each side worked together and agreed on what had happened, and that the report of the damage and the casualties was the same, that each side had a copy that was the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And so the report contained a report on the damage of what, in the village, and ...

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Damage to the houses; livestock; property; casualties, dead and wounded; and missing people who had been taken as prisoners or had just up and gone.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, could you look at Exhibit 1351, please. Have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have, on Sunday.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Who's the author of the document?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Siljeg.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Moving back to the front page, to whom is this document addressed?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the Presidency of the HVO Croatian Defence Council of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna in Mostar, the government of the HVO HZ HB in Mostar, defence department of HVO HZ HB in Mostar, and the General Staff of the HVO HZ HB in Mostar, and his own headquarters in Tomislavgrad.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And what kind of document is this?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This, again, is a situation report.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And what's the date of this report?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The actual report is dated the 20-something of January, 1993, and it refers to the situation as it was on the 28th of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, Witness, there's a couple of questions I want to ask about this document, and I first want you to have a look on page 2, and look at the bottom of this page. I'll read out the sentence. It says: "Civilian Franjo Djodjo from Prozor was also captured, of whom they allege to know nothing. When we told him what that we know who captured him and that the commander is from the ranks of the BH army, has family in Croatia and that the Irish method would be very uncomfortable, they found Franjo Djodjo in five minutes." Now, what I'm particularly interested in here is this reference to "the Irish method." Do you know what that means, "the Irish method"?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Irish method refers to a particular type of punishment shooting that the IRA used to carry out. It's called knee-capping, where you would lie a victim on the floor, face down, and shoot them through the back of the knee with a pistol.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, moving to page number 3, it starts here with, "... the subcommission toward the villages per request and determine the situation in those sectors which are enclosing the report of subcommission Gornji Vakuf, 28 January 1993." Now, what follows, would that be the type of report of a joint commission that you've been just talking about?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it would.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, as you can see, this particular report deals with the villages of Uzricje, Dusa, Trnovaca, Lucani and Gornja Ricica. Do you recall whether you were a member of this joint commission, visiting these particular villages?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall the actual villages I went to, but I would have taken the third copy from the UNPROFOR person who had been to each of these villages. Not only did each side have a copy, but we had a copy as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: So each of these reports would have gone through your hands?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Okay. Just staying on page number 3. The village of Uzricje, do you recall whether you ever visited village of Uzricje?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did visit the village of Uzricje. I did visit all of the villages in the area several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry to interrupt, but the witness mentioned that they received a copy of the minutes of these joint commissions. Perhaps it would be good idea to ask the witness whether the British Army ever handed over those documents to the OTP. As we can see, this was not obtained from the British Army but from the Croatian archives. So if the British were able to collect those documents, why did they not hand them over to the Tribunal? Because, as you know, the Croatian archives became completely accessible at the beginning of 2000, whereas --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I'll ask the witness the question. You've just heard Defence counsel. To the best of your knowledge, did the British Army hand over documents coming from these joint commissions, to the best of your knowledge? Perhaps you don't know anything about this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The reports were added on to the daily report that I produced and appeared in the daily report, the Cheshire Regiment military information summaries. As to what happened to them after that, I do not know, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, let me just focus your attention again on page number 3, on the bottom, under point number 4. It says - and this is talking about Uzricje - "A total of 24 houses destroyed (22 torched 2 shelled)." Now, what does this tell you when it says "22 torched, 2 shelled"?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It means that the village was actually taken. The troops moved into the village and either the troops or -- the Croatians living in the village or the troops and the Croatians combined burnt the houses to stop the Muslims from coming back.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: By Uzricje, you're talking about Muslims. Do you know whether Uzricje was a Muslim village or a Croat village?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Off the top of my head, I can't recall. But that was the thing that happened on both sides.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Witness, how do you know that the purpose of the torching was to prevent Muslims from coming back?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Specific targeting. You could go into a village that had been damaged and you could see. If it was a Croat village, the Muslims houses had been damaged and the Croat houses were untouched; if it was a Muslim village, then the Muslim houses were untouched and the Croat houses had been damaged. When they set fire to the houses, because of the situation, they burnt completely; the roofs collapsed inwards and everything. So there would be no way you're coming back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In paragraph 4, I see there are 18 houses that were destroyed, 16 that were torched, and 2 that were destroyed by the shelling. Now, that sentence, does that indicate that 16 houses were deliberately torched after the shelling, after the bombing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In which particular sequence it happened I can't say, Your Honour, but the ones that are torched are deliberately torched.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm just looking, because I think you were referring to the English page number 5, which relates to Dusa rather than Uzricje. Just to clarify the record, what we were talking about before was Uzricje and that your reference to paragraph 4 was regarding Dusa.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: But just to come back one more time to Uzricje and focus your attention on page 4, on the top. Under point 5, it says, "Looted two tractors and seven luxury cars." Now, what did that mean to you when vehicles were looted from a village? Did that mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It usually indicated that the people who had attacked the village were from outside of the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Very well. Let's move on, then, to the village --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A moment ago, I mentioned the sentence relating to the village of Dusa. Now, number 4, for the Dusa village, we see 24 houses destroyed; it says 22 torched and 2 shelled, destroyed with shells. Now, what conclusion can one draw? The 22 houses, were they torched? And 2 were bombed? Is that right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that's correct. Twenty-two of the houses, as it says, were torched. That means that they were deliberately set on fire at close range. And two of them had been destroyed by shell fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise, but perhaps this is the right moment to clarify something that was on page 19, line 8. The witness said that there were situations where the houses were set fire to by Croats who lived in those villages, that is to say, not the members of the HVO. So could we clarify that point?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Witness. You, yourself, were you an eyewitness of Croatian houses being at the time fire to by Croats themselves?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. This came up in the cease-fire negotiations as to -- and with the joint commission as to who would have actually done the damage. In some instances it was the HVO who'd done the damage; in some instances it was the armija who'd done it; in some instances it was the actual civilians who lived in the village themselves who turned on their neighbours and did it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, if I could just move your attention now to the village of Dusa, starting on page 4. Let me focus your attention on page 5, under number 3, which says the following: "Civilians were killed as a result of a shelling," and it names a list of five names. Do you recognise any of these names that are listed here?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recognise, line 1, Babeheta Behio and the two children.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: What do you remember about this?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This particular incident was actually brought up several times in the cease-fire negotiations. The house that they were in - and they were either in a downstairs room or in the cellar, I think it was the cellar - the house had been hit with an anti-tank round fired by a tank or fired by an anti-tank gun. It had penetrated the wall, where the wall joins onto the ground. It penetrated just above that and it killed them inside the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And did you actually see yourself the damage to that wall, or how did you know about this?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was -- again, like I said, it was brought up several times in the cease-fire negotiations. Yes, I did see it. And there was also a photograph of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: So you did see it yourself, with your own eyes, in Dusa at the house?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Which village it was, I'm not exactly sure. But, yes, I did see the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And for you there was no doubt that looking at -- looking at the damage, that this was damage caused by a fire from a tank?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Either a tank or an anti-tank gun. It had been hit by an anti-tank round. The damage to the wall and how it had hit, it was indicative that it was either a tank round or an anti-tank -- from a tank or from an anti-tank gun.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Well, these are both arms that could have direct fire; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are, yes. They are direct-fire weapon systems. You would aim at a target through a sight.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Could I just focus your attention on page 7 of this report. Again, near the bottom, and I'll read out the sentence: "Pavo Posavac, from the village of Dusa, allegedly fired from a recoilless gun on the house of Enver Sljivo in which his wife and children were killed (we did not have a recoilless gun there)." What is a recoilless gun?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: A recoilless gun is an anti-tank gun, as opposed to having a proper breech block, like artillery or whatever. It has what is called a venture on the back and there is a back blast-out as well as the round going forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And just going back to page number 5, under points 4 and 5, would your comments be again the same as regards to Uzricje, as far as the destruction of the houses is concerned and the looting of the vehicles here?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In what way? The --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Well, in the way -- when it says here that 16 were torched and two houses were destroyed by shelling, that's, in fact, something you know when you explained how these houses were torched, that that was in a similar way.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Just one other thing on this document, which is starting at the bottom of page 7, and I'll again read it out to you: "Before the situation in Gornji Vakuf, Vlado Rajic abused and decapitated an invalid. He was taken to Mostar, released, returned to Gornji Vakuf, and contributed to such a situation." Now, is this something that refers to the Vlado Rajic which we've been discussing before, about the incident on the decapitation?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it is. This was a very serious bone of contention between the two sides during the -- when we were trying to get them to stop fighting, was the fact that this HVO soldier had not been prosecuted and put in gaol. He had, in fact, been released and returned to Gornji Vakuf to take part in the fighting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I find the words "and contributed to such a situation" entirely unclear. Could, perhaps, the interpreters read or could someone read the original and then the interpreter tell us what it is supposed to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: I don't know if Your Honours want me to read the original. I don't know how good my B/C/S is. I can give it a try. I don't know if -- maybe we can ask one of the interpreters to look at the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A volunteer. We have one. Yes, Ms. Nozica.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May I be of assistance. In the original, it does not say "this situation, to such a situation," it says "to this kind of situation, such a situation." That's the only difference. Now, which situation is referred to we'll have to clear up in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, yesterday when we were discussing the military police, you were referring to the village of Hrasnica, and maybe just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're moving on, are you? Before you do that, I'd like to stay with the document, and let us take a look at page 2, Witness, in English. Right at the top of page 2, where it is stated that: "In the village of Bistrica, an HVO sniper killed two and wounded two BH army soldiers. And from the Krc facility, an HVO sniper wounded a BH army soldier in Gornji Vakuf." Now, you, yourself, did you see in the field any HVO snipers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I personally did not see any HVO snipers, Your Honour, but they did have snipers. And I think this part of the document is referring to the difficulties that both sides were having in getting renegade elements of their forces under control. We would have a fairly substantial cease-fire in position, but there were still renegade elements who would still carry on fighting. And I think that's what he's referring to there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, in fact, Colonel Siljeg, in his report, in the following sentence, says that: "In our units there are individuals who are obstructing the work of the commission working towards a cease-fire." Now, when you were part of the commission, because you attended meetings, this type of event, was it brought to the attention of UNPROFOR? And, if so, did you ask the responsible individuals what they did to punish the HVO sniper? Did you ever ask for accountability? Did you ask the military authorities how they dealt with the problem, what they did about it? Because the Colonel says that there were two HVO snipers who obstructed the cease-fire. Now, my first question is: Did you know about these events; and secondly, did you ask what was done about them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did know about the events, Your Honour. They were brought to the attention of both factions at the meetings, and each time they used to say, "Yes, we'll get it under control," but what they actually did I'm not aware of, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, yesterday you briefly discussed the village of Hrasnica when we were talking about the military police. Did you ever visit this village?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on numerous occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And were these visits both before and after?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, can you briefly explain again to the Court what happened in the village of Hrasnica.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hrasnica was attacked on at least three occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you. Hrasnica, is this a Muslim village or a Croat village?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a Muslim village.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was attacked on at least three occasions. Each attack was progressively worse than the attack before. The first time it was attacked, the civilian population just ran away. The village was damaged but still inhabitable, and the civilian population moved back. It was then attacked a second time and this time it was burnt as well, but the civilian population again moved back. So on the third time, it was completely levelled. It was bulldozed, blown up, and booby-trapped with mines. It was a -- although it was a Muslim village, it was of tactical importance to the HVO's battle plan for Gornji Vakuf in that it overlooked the road from Gornji Vakuf to Bugojno. While that village was there, they would not be able to secure the road. And also, it was the route where armija fighters from Travnik and places -- such places were coming in on foot to reinforce Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, do you know what happened with the civilian population from Hrasnica when they eventually had to move out of the village? Do you know where they went?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly where they went, but they will have moved further up towards Travnik and Novi Travnik and Bugojno, the main Muslim areas up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Could you have a look at Exhibit 1250, please. Could you tell us what kind of document is this?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a Cheshire Regiment military information summary for the 21st of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Could I focus your attention on page number 3. On the heading of "Gornji Vakuf," maybe you could just read out -- read it for yourself and tell us whether this was, in fact, a report on the attack on the village of Hrasnica.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this was one of the attacks on Hrasnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, you discussed this yesterday as well, but it says here that "the HVO soldiers responsible were believed to be wearing blue helmets and to be equipped with three BTR-40's." And then it says, as a comment, "GV believe that these soldiers may have been from Herzegovinian military police unit." That's what you testified yesterday as well, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And would you recall whether this would have been the first, the second, or the third attack?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This will have been, looking at the date and who was involved in it, will have been either the second or the third attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Finally, Witness, there is one more village that I would like to ask you questions about which is the village of Zdrimci. Do you know this village?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Did you visit the village?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: On numerous occasions throughout the six months that I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Is it a Croat village, a Muslim village, or a mixed village?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall exactly without checking as to which one it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: What can you say about the destruction of this village, when you say that you visited this village?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was, again, like all of the villages in the immediate vicinity. It had suffered some damage.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And do you remember whether Muslim houses or Croat houses were damaged in this particular village?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, it was a mixed village that was predominantly Croatian, and it was the Muslim houses that had been destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, how could you tell if you would visit a mixed village? If some of the houses were destroyed and others weren't, how could you tell that the Muslims houses were destroyed rather than the Croat houses?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer to this may sound bizarre, but the three ethnic groups tended to build houses with a different shaped roof which then would indicate which ethnic group lived in that house. So you could go into a village and you could tell by looking at the houses, the roofs, whether the houses that were intact were Croatian or Muslim or Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, one last exhibit that I would like to ask you to look at, which is exhibit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's the first time I hear about this. Could you tell us what the rooftops looked like? What was their shape?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't remember which group built the roof which way, but some of them -- one side, it was like a pyramid-type shape with just four triangles; the others were similar but with a flat roof. But they tended to build the roof of a particular style, depending on which ethnic group they belonged to. I don't know why they did that, really.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps not to waste the time on the cross. This is the whole story, and we agree this is the kind of rule. But there's too many exceptions, and I guess the witness knows that. So if you would ask him additional questions, to avoid that subject matter on the cross, I think that would help a lot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to Mr. Kovacic, Defence counsel, what you are saying, in general terms, seems to be true, but there might have been exceptions. What do you think of this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There will have been exceptions caused primarily by the movements of refugees. It was a general rule. It was correct the majority of the time. In addition, with the commission, the joint commissions, you could -- the village -- when we checked the villages, the one ethnic group had disappeared out of the village, which also confirmed that one particular ethnic group in that village had gone.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Just a follow-up question on this. I mean, if this joint commission would visit a village and would report on these damaged houses, would they only base their assessment on the type of roof, whether this was a Muslim house or a Croat house, or also another aspects?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The joint commission logged all the damage in the village irrespective of whose house had been damaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm not really understanding your answer here. Maybe my question wasn't clear. How would the joint commission know whether a house was a Muslim house or a Croat house?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: When they were in the village, they would speak to the local population in the village and ask them whether they were Croat -- well, they knew most of the time whether they were Croat or Muslim, and try to find out where the other part of the village had gone.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, maybe one last exhibit, which is 1373. What kind of document is this?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, this is a Cheshire Regiment military information summary for the 31st of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, if you move to page 2 of this report, what's been reported here, would this be, again, part of a report from a joint commission?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And is it correct that, under A, a report has been given about --

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a report about the village of Zdrimci.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And just to finish this off, maybe could you just read out what's been said about the village of Zdrimci.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: "This village was reported to be mixed but under HVO control. There were approximately 100 Muslims, predominantly old people, women and children, all of whom wished to leave. During the conflict, two Muslims and three Croats were reported to have been killed, and six Muslims wounded. 31 young Muslim males were currently reported to be detained; 19 were in a local prison and 12 were held at Prozor in order to be used for a prison exchange. 33 Muslim houses were reported to have been destroyed during the conflict."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. This concludes my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, you give me the countdown and tell me how much the Prosecution has had yesterday and today. The Defence teams will have the same amount of time. Before we have a break in 20 minutes' time, I shall give the floor to the first Defence counsel. Who is to take the floor first?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the Prosecutor referred to Pusic in a paragraph. He has not been accused of anything in the indictment, so we cede our time to the other Defence teams.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You were questioned twice by the Prosecutor before; is that correct? You've given two statements.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've given one statement for this trial, and I gave an earlier statement for a trial some years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Correct. And then you testified in Kordic as well.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I testified in that trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And, of course, before coming here today, it would appear, at least, that on Sunday, or maybe Saturday, or Saturday and Sunday, you met with the gentleman there.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I met with the Prosecutor on Sunday.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: May I ask, just out of curiosity, how many hours did you meet with him? Or was it --

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what time we started, but we finished at about 3.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And I take it at that point in time he showed you documents you had never seen?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And did he let you read through the documents or did he point to specific areas and told you that he would be asking you questions or asking you to verify the contents of those portions?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: He asked me for how -- the certain paragraphs of certain parts of certain documents, how that fitted in with the situation in Gornji Vakuf at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. I take it he also allowed you or gave you the opportunity to read the entire document, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't allowed to read the whole thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No? Okay. Well, documents that were generated by, for instance, the HVO, did you ask to look at the other documents to, perhaps, see whether they may contain some information that would allow you to put the matters into perspective, into a proper context?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Would you agree with me that, perhaps, some of those documents would contain information that you were totally unaware of, in spite of your position as an intelligence officer?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, parts of those documents I would be unaware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, speaking about your function, as I understand from the Kordic trial, at the time that you were there, you were a colour sergeant?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a sergeant at the start of the tour and I got promoted during the tour to colour sergeant.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm from the United States and we have master sergeants, gunny sergeants, you know. Is that just one rank up, sergeant, or is that the top of the level?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. A colour sergeant is one rank below a sergeant major.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. I'm familiar a little bit with the US Army, you know, and normally sergeants are not in the business of intelligence. You would have, perhaps, a warrant officer who's trained in that position. So if I could ask, were you train as an intelligence officer?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have been on intelligence courses and I was -- I did intelligence gathering in East Tyrone, in Northern Ireland, and also in South Armagh.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And this was before your tour over here?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You had no prior experience in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We were the first unit to deploy --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- into Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And I take it that was your first -- your personal first time exposed to that particular area.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: In other words, you hadn't gone to Dubrovnik at some point on vacation.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, before coming into the situation, I take it that you were briefed somewhat.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were briefed a little. There was not much information really known at a low level on the ground, what it was actually like on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had reconnaissance teams, who deployed a few weeks before we deployed, to gather some information. But their main task, really, was to find somewhere for us to be accommodated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, now, you've piqued my curiosity a little bit. I know that there were, sort of, British special forces running around throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina during the war. Are we talking about those fellows or are we talking about just a unit that went there to look for where you would be billeted, how to make sure that it's a proper and safe area?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was our reconnaissance teams, from inside our regiment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you said you were briefed a little bit. When you say "a little bit," you know, that's like asking "How long is a string?" So how little is "a little bit"?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was literally a couple of hours on the actual situation on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well --

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Primarily, at that stage, we hadn't deployed. Our mission was to escort aid convoys. As far as we were concerned, the war was between the Serbs on one side and the Muslims and Croats on the other and had nothing to do with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. But this little bit of training or little bit of briefing that you got, was that primarily on the terrain itself?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ground training.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But with respect to, you know, the political situation, the reasons why the situation was going on, was that part of the briefing or was that something incidental?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was part of the briefing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The army intelligence corps even produced a magazine called "Threat" in which they -- it was probably about 20 pages long, which was a brief history of Yugoslavia and the effect of the death of Tito and how it just crumbled.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Well, Yugoslavia is a big place. You were now in Bosnia and in particular one area. But with respect to that particular area, how much briefing did you get?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Virtually none.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. That was what I was asking for, actually. Now, yesterday you did enlighten us a little bit about the importance of that particular area to both sides. Was that something that you came to find out once you got there or is that something that you knew in advance?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was something we came to find out once we got there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And, of course, you being a military man, in intelligence and in your other experiences, you could look at the map and you could tell the importance of controlling that particular area.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Were you also, at any point in time, given any information with respect to Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very little. Again, when we initially deployed, I first went -- I was in Vitez for one day, and then went down to Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Was that geopolitically or politically or militarily important, that area, Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, it was to do with routes. You need routes for the lorries.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, you need routes for the lorries, but were there any, like, ammunition depots or batteries that might have been important to one side or the other?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, there was some sort of arms factory somewhere around the Travnik area, somewhere around there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And that might make that area rather significant to either side --

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: -- right? Okay. Now, you got to the theatre at what point in time? What was the exact month; do you recall?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: November.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: November. Now, that --

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, it was either late October or early November.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, had some events occurred prior to your arrival in that area?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: There'd been some incidents in Prozor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. What about a little bit before that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, there had been some fighting, had there not, between the Croats and Muslims against the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, against the Serbs, yes. But, by and large, the front lines in that area were static.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You told us that a little bit yesterday. In fact, there was one particular place that fell; right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And that was?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Jajce.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And with the falling of Jajce, was there not a significant movement of population?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Known as refugees; right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Do you happen to know the number?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't, I'm afraid. It was outside of my area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, did you ever learn of it?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, in intelligence, might that be an important number, for instance? I'm not trying to put you on the spot, and I'll tell you why. Yesterday, you told us a little bit about the TOs, Territorial Defences; right? Militias, you called them, I believe. You were aware, obviously, being in intelligence, that every male of a military age was, in effect, mobilised?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right? You're shaking your head. That means yes?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. We have to make a record.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And so that would make every male, irrespective of where he is, subject -- whatever side, whatever ethnic or national make-up, subject to recruitment; right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And so with this large number of refugees, might it have been important for you, for instance, to learn how many able-bodied men were there that had come from Jajce or other places that could be recruited by either side?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did have the figures of refugees. I just cannot recall what they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I'm not talking about refugees now. You see, I switched. I'm now talking about able-bodied men, because that's the count that you would actually use, would you not, being in intelligence, as to how many able-bodied soldiers there might be on one side or the other? Right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And would it be not -- also, you talked a little bit about the TOs yesterday. You didn't go too much into it. But if I understand the concept of a TO and you used the word "militia," we're talking about home-grown [static on English channel]. They're there to locally protect what is theirs and around themselves; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But now, with the influx of refugees and large numbers of able-bodied men - and, incidentally, I'm sure you know the figure is -- the age bracket is, I think, 16 or 18 to 60 or 65 - now you're in a situation where you would have a large number of able-bodied men who would also be able to be used as a mobile unit; right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And, of course, if that large number of able-bodied men happened to be Muslim - and, in fact, we have heard some testimony here that there were large numbers of refugees with able-bodied men from that area - that would now provide the ABiH with a rather significant increase in its manpower; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it would.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, you can imagine, can you not, in looking at that map, I believe it was the President who was quite keen on showing us and pointing out how the villages are mixed all over the place; right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Some villages are mixed and then you have other villages which are basically homogenous. But, in essence, they're all over the place, intermingled; right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And with the large number of Muslims coming now as refugees, able-bodied men, would it not, in your opinion, as a military man, as a career man, would that not cause some concern, some concern to the Croats?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It did cause some concern to the Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. But when we say it did, that's a realistic feeling, is it not?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They did actually -- they mentioned it several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. But, I mean, they were not being irrational about it, given the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they would be being irrational about it, because nominally they were allies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, hold on. Let's think about this slowly. They were nominally allies. As I understand from your testimony in Kordic, you say that, you know, they would have these cease-fires, they would break them, back, on and on; right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So it was a sort of a forced marriage, as you will, forced by the situation of what was happening from the Serbs, but they didn't trust each other; right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they didn't trust each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And they did have problems with each other.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did have problems; however, the two commanders of each side locally within Gornji Vakuf did actually have quite a good relationship.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: They tried very hard. And you even told us today that there were these renegade elements and, to use the terms that were used by the Prosecutor yesterday which drew my objection, it would appear, at least from your testimony today, that the commanders did not always have effective command and control over their units; right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was prevalent right the way through. The commanders at all levels could not control their men properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So, in spite - in spite - their best efforts, their best intentions, their willingness to work with each other and try to find some common ground within this madness, this war, they were not able to control individuals that had, you know, perhaps, their own agenda, whatever that agenda may be; right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, getting back to the irrationality, you know, given the situation - and it would appear to me, the only thing that comes to my mind is somewhat of a tinder box situation, you know - these large numbers of able-bodied men coming in, that's not -- that would heighten the anxiety of these people, would it -- of the Croats, would it not?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it would.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, we talked about -- you talked about the significance of this area, and it would seem to me that we can't talk about one side without really thinking about the other side as well; right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: In other words, if it's relevant and important for the Croats to control this area, we could equally say the same thing about the Muslims; right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's perfectly true. Both sides knew the significance of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And both sides were playing for the field; right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In what way?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, both sides wanted to control it in one way or the other.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the HVO wanted to actually take control of it for themselves. The armija, on the other hand, just wanted it open as a route --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and were prepared to let anybody use it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, you know, you say that, and first I want to remind you that on page 6056 in your Kordic testimony - this was on 2 August 1999 - you said something that cause my attention. It says that you were -- you know -- well, you were asked a question, and it was: "You found yourself confronted with a confusing and complex situation militarily and ethnically and politically." That was the question. It starts on line 18. And you say "Yes." Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And from what we heard initially, you virtually were not necessarily briefed, at least not comprehensively, in order to make sense of this confusing, complex situation, militarily, ethnically and politically; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right at the very beginning, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, you were billeted in that area; right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in a factory on the edge of the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And might I ask whether you had Croats or Muslims as your interpreters?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We, at the start, had both. Once the troubles broke out, we were left with just two, two Muslim sisters, and a captain in the British Army who could speak Serbo-Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you say "we." That would be you as well.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So whenever you went there -- and that was your ears basically; right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Because you didn't speak the language.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, I noticed something, incidentally, in both of your statements that you gave, that there's -- I don't want to say "nothing" because that would be uncharitable. But there's virtually nothing there with respect to what the Muslims were doing. In other words, all the information that you are imparting is against the Serbs -- I mean, against the Croats. Now, would that be a fair characterisation?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the start of our deployment, we were there -- our actual mission was the route, to keep the route open, and we did not have problems with the Muslims to keep the route open. When we did have problems, it was the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Apparently I didn't make myself clear. In reading your statements, okay, it would appear -- and I have to say this with some degree of regret, that it almost came out yesterday, no fault of your own, that when the questions were being posed, it was all against what the Croats were doing without anything coming from the other side; in other words, as if the Muslims were not doing anything and they were strictly being attacked by the Croats. Would one get that impression when reading your two statements?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said to your last question, we were there to -- initially to keep that route open, and the problems that we had in trying to keep it open were caused, 9 times out of 10, by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
