utterances.text: All right. Let me go about it another way. You were questioned by the Prosecutor on two occasions; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, they were obviously seeking information from you, you being on the ground; right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And it would appear that if you wanted to be fair about it, or if they wanted to be fair about it - and I can't vouch for that one way or the other - but if they wanted to be fair and if you wanted to be fair, you would be talking about both sides; right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Step by step, we're going to get there. I'm trying to help you out here. Work with me. Now, it would appear that if you're trying to -- if you're trying to understand the situation, you can't understand it in the abstract; right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And so if we're talking about a particular situation, there's usually action and there's reaction; right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And what I'm trying to say to you - and perhaps I'm just being inarticulate because I'm tired - that when I read your statements, it appears that you never say whatever the Muslims might have been doing, or the ABiH; in other words, one would walk away with the impression that the Croats were constantly on the offensive and the ABiH was simply either on the defensive or doing nothing or incapable of doing anything.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's two things. First of all, like I said, we were there primarily to keep the route open, and the problems that we had keeping the route open were nearly always caused by the HVO. And secondly, the armija did not attack Gornji Vakuf --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- the HVO did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, we're going to talk about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right now I believe it's time for the break, Your Honours, but I'll just touch on a few more issues and then -- because I know I have limited time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, could you tell me how much time Mr. Karnavas has had so far? It is now a quarter to 4.00. We shall have a 20-minute break and resume at five minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, I've been told that you've used up 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Twenty-two. I just have a few more minutes. I could cross-examine the gentleman for hours, but I'll just cover the few points.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We left off when you said that it was the Croats that attacked Gornji Vakuf. Now, in your previous testimony - and, again, this is on page 6067, dated 2 August 1999, when you testified in Kordic - you said that it was hard to put an exact time and date as to when it started, because it was sporadically occurring at the time, that is, the fighting; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were a series of clashes and it built up from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And that was well before the 15th of January.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: There'd been sporadic clashes in the previous year, even before our deployment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Exactly. And those sporadic clashes, do you know who was initiating each and every clash?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because at that particular time, the main effort was the route itself, not what the warring factions were doing with each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: In other words, it might be the Muslims one time; it might be the Croats another time. Tit for tat, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was evidence that a lot of it was tit for tat.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And that had been ongoing before you got there, while you were there, and then, of course, after the so-called ultimatum; right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want to move to another area. The Prosecution has spent quite a bit of time on that individual Vlatko Rajic who beheaded the Muslim, and you told us that there was some concern that after he went to Mostar he returned from there.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did you actually see that individual?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't see the individual.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. But you were just told of that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, did you, as an intelligence officer, ever make any efforts to go to Mostar or to use your sources in Mostar to see whether there had been any Prosecution of this individual; and, if so, what might have been the result?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because it was completely outside of the British area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Yet it would appear, at least from your testimony, that this is the sort of thing that keeps being mentioned all the time as a significant event; right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was significant in that -- first of all, that it happened, and then that situation calmed down, and then it was significant in that it came up during the cease-fire talks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, at this point in time, perhaps I can hand you -- for your convenience we could have the -- and we can either -- we can use the e-court as well, but I just want to make sure we cover this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: May I ask a question on this same Rajic issue. You have said, sir, that the issue came up in cease-fire talks. On those occasions, did the representatives of the HVO usually deny that Rajic had returned? Was this contested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it wasn't contested, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: In fact, let me make sure that we get your testimony absolutely clear, because yesterday you said it was neither confirmed, nor denied; right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me just -- I'm short of time. And you being in intelligence, you know sometimes, when you're having these negotiations, neither confirming or denying is a tactic or a ploy that is used, because there is no sense in giving away your positions; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So nothing nefarious. In other words, to make sure that our Judges know, you were warning them: Your denial to answer this question can and will be used later on, at least presumptively, as an admission that this person wasn't prosecuted, is back in the field, and is back doing harm. Right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: There was no -- okay. Fine. Now, if we could look at document 1D 00943, a document that you haven't seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And for the Court --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: The Prosecution did not receive a copy of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It should be in the e-court. And if I may, Your Honour, this is a --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: We don't have it in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It should be in e-court. If not, we will have to give the gentleman -- we'll give an extra copy to the gentleman. If we could look at that. Just by way of introduction, I had my investigator check in Mostar, and we're going to go through several documents, and what I will demonstrate, at least through these documents, is that the gentleman was, indeed -- the prosecutor was, indeed, in custody this entire time, and contrary to what was believed at the time during these negotiations, and contrary to what the Prosecution would have us believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If you could look at the first document. It's dated 9 April 1993. Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And it says here that this is a decision, does it not?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we could flip to the second page, because we don't have much time, and I'm going to read from the first paragraph on the second page, in the middle, where it says: "Namely, investigation against the accused is under way due to the well-grounded suspicion that he committed a criminal act from Article 36, paragraph 2, item 3, of the Criminal Code of RBiH, and this criminal act is punishable with death sentence. Therefore, based on Article 191, paragraph 1, of the Law on Criminal Procedure, detention must be imposed on the accused. The investigation has not been concluded due to objective reasons which the first-instance court justifiably concluded and applied the law properly." Does it not say that, sir?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And the Court will have ample time to go through this. Again, I apologise for not going step by step, but, of course, you're not a lawyer either, are you?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we go to the next document, 1D 00944. If you look at this, it's dated 21 February 1995. If we look on the fourth line, we see the name Vlatko Rajic.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That would be the same Rajic, would it not? At least it would appear.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it would.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. This is a decision, too, and if I may just read the first part, it says under the decision: "The security measure of obligatory psychiatric treatment and custody in a medical institution pronounced to Vlatko Rajic," and it goes on about his son, and what have you. That would be the same Vlatko Rajic, would it not?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it would.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And then, again, I'm going to have to just skip through. It would appear, if we look at this document, look at the second page, it would appear that the whole issue is whether he, at this particular time, is going to seek treatment while in custody or out of custody. And if we go to the second paragraph on page 2, in the middle of it, it says -- I'll just read the whole thing: "Having considered the above listed, the court agrees with the measure proposed by the expert neuropsychiatrist, who has given his expert opinion about the personality of the accused after he talked to him, and the opinion agrees, to a certain extent, with the report of the District Prison in Mostar. Having in mind all the above stated, the court hold justifiable the request of the accused that the security measure pronounced to him be abolished and that he be pronounced security measure of obligatory psychiatric treatment at liberty as of 1 March 1995 ..." And it goes on, so on and so forth. From here, would it not be fair to say that we can conclude that, at least as of this particular period, he was still in custody?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you could conclude that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. In other words, he could not be in two places at one time; one in custody and at the other time in Gornji Vakuf, as was being touted by the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have a look at page 1 of the decision, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In paragraph 3 there, "Exposition," if we read the paragraphs, it would appear that on the 26th of January, the person concerned underwent psychiatric treatment, and perhaps he left after that, because psychiatric treatment is in a medical institution, not a prison necessarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I don't -- well, I think we can -- I don't see where -- well, let me put it to you this way, Your Honour, because we're short of time: This individual has agreed to come and testify before this Court, so we can hear from him and he can tell us whether he was in -- I'm told by my investigator that he indicated that he was in -- in custody throughout this time. But we will bring this gentleman to put this matter at rest. And if we could look at the last document, 1D 00945.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: This appears to be a certificate, does it not, dated 28 February 1995?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And, again, you being not a lawyer, there is no need to go into it. I know I'm short of time. If I can ask one or two questions more. I notice when you gave evidence in the Kordic case, you, as a security officer or in the security business, intelligence business, you were placing emphasis that Siljeg was communicating with Split because the number that was being used -- or on occasion he had used the fax machine with that number; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: He'd made a number of faxes, and the number that he dialed had a Split area code.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. But from that, it would appear that you had -- you were intimating that he was communicating with folks in Split, were you not?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I just reported that he was --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- it was a Split area code.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. But you're not claiming that he was -- because you were asked where Split was and you said it was in Croatia, so one might get the impression that you were trying to convey the impression that he was actually communicating with authorities in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was -- it was -- he was using -- he was faxing to a number and the number had the Split prefix.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I suspect you, being in intelligence, knew by then that in Mostar there were several numbers with a Split prefix; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Early on in that stage, we only knew certain numbers. We didn't know all the numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. But the question was: There were certain numbers in Mostar with a Split prefix.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Well, I'm terribly sorry that we don't have time to have a more convivial discourse on all of these matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will do for now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Next.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Williams.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: My name is Peter Murphy. I'm one of the lawyers representing Mr. Bruno Stojic. Mr. Karnavas asked you a few questions about the briefing that you received before taking up your deployment, and I think you responded that it was very little.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: In fact, when you gave a statement to the Prosecutor, you indicated that the briefing had been carried out by a person called Martin Bell; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Martin Bell was a personal friend of Colonel Bob Stewart and at that time was on leave, after having been injured in an incident in Sarajevo, and he came and spoke to the officers and senior NCOs of the regiment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And Colonel Bob Stewart was the commanding officer of the regiment or that part of the regiment?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Bob Stewart commanded the 1st Battalion of the Cheshire Regiment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And Martin Bell, in fact, is a television journalist, is he not?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is a journalist for the BBC.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And it was Mr. Bell who was brought in to give you a briefing.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He came of his own free will, as a favour to Colonel Stewart, and spoke to, primarily, the officer and also some NCOs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: All right. Now, are you acquainted with an officer, who then had the rank of major, called Jacqueline Carter?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: You don't remember that she was an officer who was also a doctor, a medical doctor?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think her surname might be different at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did have a major, female.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: A female --

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: A female who was a doctor, but her last name wasn't Carter, I don't think. So maybe she's married since.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Do you know whether she was sometimes known by the name of Tracy?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: All right. Now, I bring her up because I want to ask you a few questions about the various documents you've been asked about, particularly the information summaries and then the milinfo documents. You testified yesterday that you were the person who would write the material that went into the info summary; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would right most of the material from the Gornji Vakuf area; not all of it but most of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And that information, or what you wrote, would then be passed up the line to Vitez.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, where it would be absorbed into the milinfosums that you've seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Do you know a captain by the name of Robbie Boyd? Does that name mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Captain Boyd was our company operations officer, as I recall, and he was attached to us from the Royal Irish Regiment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Was Captain Boyd with you throughout the time that you were deployed in Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, he was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: I mention him because when Lieutenant Colonel Carter, as she now is, gave evidence to the Judges, she said that Captain Boyd was the one who prepared the infosums and that you would do it on occasion.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. Captain Boyd would compile the situation report, the sitrep. I would compile the milinfosum.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: So, Lieutenant Colonel Carter was mistaken about that when she said that, then.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: She was mistaken. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: All right. Now, you said, in answer to Mr. Karnavas, that you began the deployment as a sergeant. You were then promoted to colour sergeant.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: So you were a non-commissioned officer.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: A senior non-commissioned officer, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: A senior NCO, yes. And above you, there were -- in addition to Captain Boyd, and I think this is the first time we've heard about him this afternoon, there was also, as you've said, first of all, your commander -- the commander of the unit or battalion -- I'm not sure what his title is, but Major Rule at first and then Major Jones?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were the officers commanding B Company.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Officer commanding B Company. And then below those officers, you had Captain Short, who spoke B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: In fact, he was a military interpreter. That was his job, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And also a Captain Hughes, who you said was the liaison officer with the HVO.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the liaison officer for B Company. He liaised with both the HVO and the armija.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Obviously, by definition, all the people that I've mentioned were superior in rank to you.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Now, as far as the actual negotiations with local commanders went, if you were trying to achieve a cease-fire or to bring about a deal of some kind, that would be done by the officer commanding Major Rule or Major Jones; right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On most occasions, yes, it was, and on some occasions, when there were higher-ranking HVO or armija at the negotiations, we would have higher-ranking people as well, as a sign of respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Because, in general, it would be appropriate to have communications with local officers conducted by officers of approximately the same rank, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And if the commanding officers were not involved, then, would most of the negotiation be done by either Captain Hughes or by Captain Short?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Within the base itself, when we had the local commanders in, it would be done by the OC, Major Rule or Major Jones, with probably at least one of them present. Sometimes I was in there and interpreters, a clerk. Not Major Clark. A clerk, clerk.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: But your role would be, essentially, to assist the officers in conducting those meetings or negotiations, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: They would sometimes ask me to go and get bits of information out of the files.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: So would it be right to say that quite a bit of the information that would go into the reports that you wrote would, in fact, be relayed to you by the officers who were conducting those meetings rather than things that you, yourself, had observed.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it would be correct to say that. Some of it was gleaned from the interpreters; some of it, I was present in the room when it was said and wrote it down; and some of it, I wasn't present and it was relayed to me afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Because, in addition to your role as an intelligence officer, you also had what I could call a more normal military position as a mortar team leader?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mortar fire controller.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: You are also a trained medic, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: I have to ask you this, something that we were told by Dr. Carter. You don't play in the band as well, do you?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I understand where you're coming from on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: That was not too serious a question. One other thing. You mentioned that, in assessing intelligence, you had a designation of its credibility which went from A1 to F6.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You had A, B, C, D, E, F, and 1 to 6, so you could be A6 or B3 or whatever, and it depended on how it correlated with other information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Because, in relation to one report that was mentioned yesterday concerning an information you got from a mercenary, it was said that there was a question about the reliability of the information.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was graded F6 because there was no way of actually checking it. We didn't actually have any other source of information to compare it against.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Who would be -- within B Company, who would be responsible for attaching the designation of reliability to a particular piece of information?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Either myself or, later on, an assistant I had called Sergeant Peter Dalton.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: So that would not be something that was done by one of the commissioned officers?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at my level. Higher up in Vitez they would regrade it all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: All right. Now, I wanted to ask you about one specific matter that you mentioned yesterday. This was, for the record, on page 57 of the transcript. You were asked some questions about the presence of certain Muslim fighters you described as extremists, I think, within the 7th Brigade. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And was it your testimony that there was some evidence that some of these fighters within the 7th Brigade had come from foreign countries, or not?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Because you were asked, I think, a specific question about the presence of the fighters known as the Mujahedin, and you said that there were no such people in your area. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Perhaps, with the assistance of the court officer, we could see a Prosecution exhibit in e-court. The number is 01210. 01210.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Okay. Do you see that, Mr. Williams?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And this document appears to be -- is headed "Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the 3rd Corps in Zenica," dated 19 January 1993, and it's headed, "Special Combat Report." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And if you look at the -- if we can go briefly to the end of the document, it's signed by somebody called Selmo Cikotic. Do you know who that is?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was the security officer for the 3rd Corps of the armija.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Okay. Now if we could go back, then, to the previous page and look at item number 3. It begins with the word "Requests." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: "That Lendo ..." -- do you know who that is?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can recall the name but I can't recall exactly where he fitted in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Would you accept that he was a commander within the armija?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: "... provide someone to get to the village of Bistrica." We've talked about that village, have we not?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: "... during the night and take over the command of the Infantry Company from Novi Travnik, the Mujahedins, and the troops from Bistrica."

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: "These are then to be used to execute an attack along the route. The check-point in the village Bistrica-Fran Kovac Kubu-Zvizde-Gornji Vakuf, to link with the forces in the town and supply us with the materiel and technical equipment located there." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Have you ever seen this document before today?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: So this was not one of the documents the Prosecution showed you on Sunday, then.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Are you aware of the attack that was being referred to in this document?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember the check-point that's referred to in that document being attacked, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: May we see another Prosecution exhibit, please. The number is 01632. 01632.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: While that's coming up, you also testified yesterday at some length about the military police, if you recall.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And what their role had been.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And, if I have this correct, you testified that you could recognise, or somebody could recognise, the military police because they had blue helmets and drove around in blue vehicles. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was correct some of the time. It's not strictly true. They did not have blue vehicles all of the time. But if the vehicles were blue, then they were military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Can you give us a little more detail about that? What type of vehicles were these that you were talking about?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: BTR 50s which are old Soviet troop carriers. Occasionally, a POV. A POV is a small armoured car with a gun platform on it, a machine-gun platform, POV 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: So these were armoured vehicles?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Light armoured vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Did they have any particular markings or insignia on them that you recall?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Is this something that you saw personally or was it information that was given to you by someone else?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: So you did actually see these vehicles.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did see some military police, yes, and some vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: On more than one occasion?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I only ever actually saw them once, personally. But other people saw them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: What kind of distance away from the vehicle were you on the occasion when you saw them?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hundred and fifty yards, 200 yards.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: You don't recall any markings or insignia or whether there were any at all.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that at all, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: You're quite sure, are you, that the military police officers that you are talking about were wearing blue helmets?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not to be confused with the UN powder blue. It's a darker blue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Important distinction. So it was --

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was noticeably different. It was far darker.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: So it was a different shade of blue; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Far darker.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Was it darker?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: All right. But there is no doubt in your mind that these people were wearing these dark blue helmets.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, some of them were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And that they were military police.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Now that we have this document, I think, in front of you -- can you see that on the screen, Mr. Williams?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: It's a report from the brigade Dr. Ante Starcevic in Gornji Vakuf, dated the 9th of March, 1993; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: On the conflict between the army of BiH and HVO in Gornji Vakuf, it says, under the word "Report."

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And if we could go to the next page of that, please. I want to go to an item under letter D. If we could scroll down to the bottom there, do you see a paragraph D, beginning "The future task of all units ..."?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: I mention this because, before I ask you a question about this, you testified yesterday that it was your impression that the HVO military police were mostly concerned to protect the Croat civilians and perhaps not quite so much the Muslim civilians. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: This paragraph D says: "The future task of all units, especially the Brigade Command with all its services and military police as well as juridical organs, is not only in defence of Croat population and areas. These tasks must be aimed at suppressing all negative occurrences in this area." And then it refers to robberies, and so on, and then the last sentence says: "Other tasks include the preservation of public peace and order, protection of lives and the property of the citizens." And then immediately below that, we can't see it, but just perhaps on the next page, it's signed by the chief of the SIS, Mr. Kolak; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Just for the record, the date of this document, you mentioned that for the record. I don't think it was mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I thought we mentioned it. I'm sorry if I didn't. It's the 9th of March, 1993, at the top of page 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: In fact, Mr. Karnavas talked to you about the particular case of Mr. Rajic who had murdered the young Muslim man. It was, in fact, the military police who had arrested Mr. Rajic, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I presume so, yes. I don't know for definite who actually arrested him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Well, in that case, could we look at another document, number -- Prosecution Exhibit P 00768. If we could see that briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Just while that's coming up, you did say that it was the HVO who had insisted that Mr. Rajic be taken to Mostar; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Muslim armija wanted him to go to Zenica, I believe --

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- to stand trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: But the HVO said he should go to Mostar, as I understand it.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: All right. Now, can you see the document in front of you there, sir?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Head "The Basic Court in Bugojno" and dated the 18th of November, 1992.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: "Record of Crime-Scene Investigation"; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Then it begins -- I don't want to read the whole thing, but it begins by saying that the record is being made by the investigating judge, "following the discovery of the headless corpse of Salih Grizic outside the house of Huso Guko." So this is the crime that we've been talking about, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And at the beginning of the next paragraph there, it says that "The armed forces military police informed us" - that would be the court - "that the murder had taken place," and so on.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: And then if you look at the bottom of that page, you see a paragraph beginning, "The team immediately went to the scene of the crime."

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: "The crime scene was secured by the members of the HVO military police --"

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: "-- who claimed that the scene of the crime was not tampered with," and so on. It also says that Mr. Rajic, the accused, had been detained at the Gornji Vakuf HVO military police prison; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: So, would you agree from that document, sir, it appears that the investigation was carried out by the military police --?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: -- is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. May I just briefly inquire how much time I have left? Can I just ask the court officer how much time I have?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, please, and Mr. Coric. THE ACCUSED CORIC: [Interpretation] I would just like to make a brief intervention. It's probably matter of the interpretation. The military police detained Mr. Rajic, in detention, not put him in prison. So those are two separate things. I think that was just a translation question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have had 22 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Just one or two very, very brief things. Going back, Mr. Williams, to the interview that you conducted with the mercenary, which we talked about before, what was the name of that gentleman that you interviewed, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was Iswelyn Llwellyn Thomas.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Llwellyn Thomas?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Iswelyn Llwellyn Thomas.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: All right. Only if you're from Wales can you pronounce that properly, I know. Was there also another mercenary you were acquainted with, a Mr. Rutter?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally knew Carl Rutter, Charles Rutter. He served in the same company as me some years before. He's an ex-soldier from our regiment. He fought in Bosnia, he fought in Mostar during the battle of Mostar, and he actually -- on one occasion, there was a problem at a Croat check-point and he appeared out of the bushes -- with one of our patrols, and he appeared out of the bushes and said, "Hi'ya lads. What's the problem?" And then he sorted it all out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: I don't want to cut you off. It's just because of the time. I just wanted to know if you were acquainted with Mr. Rutter. You know who I mean by that.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: All right. And, finally, I just have to ask you: You recall yesterday testifying about having come across some soldiers who appeared to be members of the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Split, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: In Split -- from Split who said that they were going to a wedding.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. They'd been to a wedding.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Or been to a wedding. And you commented that that must be the wedding between Herceg-Bosna and Croatia. I think we all enjoyed that line. Was that something that you came up with yourself, or did somebody else come up with that one?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I misquoted there. I asked them what they were doing there, why they were there, and they said for a wedding. Whether they'd been to a wedding or were going to a wedding, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. I assumed that they were referring to Herceg-Bosna and Croatia. They were heavily armed. They had all their weaponry with them, all their equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: During all the briefings that you received, did you ever receive any briefings on the political structure of Herceg-Bosna at all?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I can't remember it at all hardly. I know Mate Boban was the head of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: That's all I have, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next Defence counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence of Mr. Praljak will have a total of an hour and 15 minutes time. You gave us 30 minutes. We received 30 minutes from my colleague Mr. Ibrisimovic and about 15 minutes from Ms. Alaburic. I'm going to use up some of that time, and then my client will be asking questions of a purely technical and military nature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, please. Mr. Karnavas, how much time did Mr. Ibrisimovic give you?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I didn't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because Mr. Pusic is giving his time to all and everyone. So if everybody is having his time, well, then, we might still be here for weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I think we're moving along quite well, Your Honour. Now, to answer your question specifically, I just borrowed it without asking, and so -- but I would certainly -- I think that we can make some allowances on this occasion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. I'm sure Mr. Kovacic will show us how flexible he is. You need an hour and quarter; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We need at least three or four hours, but an hour and a quarter is what we were given and we will endeavour to complete our cross-examination within that time. I'm speaking on behalf of my client as well. Although, of course, we would need more time because the witness knows a great deal. He was there for six months. He could contribute a lot. But let's leave that for another occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon. My name is Bozidar Kovacic. I'm Defence counsel for Slobodan Praljak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you're going to be using up an hour and a quarter of an hour; 30 minutes which are your 30 minutes, 30 minutes which were given to you by Mr. Pusic, and 15 minutes which were given to you by Ms. Alaburic. So that's an hour and 15 minutes all in all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct, Your Honour. Yes. And we will certainly respect that time limit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you questions in Croatian. Since you'll be answering in English, we have the interpreters and I'd like to ask you to pause between question and answer to help them along. Mr. Williams, you gave two statements to the Prosecution, one in 2005, in September, and another one in May, 1995, and you -- or, rather, 2005, and you also testified in the Kordic trial. Is it true that, in neither of those statements, neither to the investigators nor your testimony, did you mention General Praljak?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's perfectly correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And if I may say, you never met him personally on any occasion. Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's also correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Williams, you have described to us, and you did so in a number of places, an event. You mentioned one when the Croatians put out the flag in the school in Gornji Vakuf and an incident broke out. You know the flag incident that I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you in that regard the following: Do you remember other similar incidents in other towns in the territory where BritBat was active? I mean similar in the sense of flags being hoisted by one side, the other side taking them down, and then an incident breaking out.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I can recall, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: If I might try and jog your memory. There was a very similar incident in Travnik, for instance, which your unit covered, the area?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, our unit did cover that area, but it wasn't within my little bit of the area. Travnik was covered from Vitez, and so it wasn't -- I was not concentrated on Travnik. I was concentrated on Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. But bearing in mind the incident that you say you remember, do you agree with me when I say that an incident like that demonstrates the general mood and atmosphere that was prevalent in Bosnia-Herzegovina, an atmosphere of tension, the wish for ethnic groups to emancipate, and so on? Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And flags quite obviously - and you noted that very well - played an important role as the symbol of each of these nations or ethnic groups. Do you agree with me there?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You do. Right. I'm sure you know Major Watters, Brian Watters. Do you know him from your mission in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Major Watters was part of my regiment and I'd known him since he was a senior lieutenant. He joint our regiment out in Bosnia towards the end of the tour in the capacity, as I recall, of Battalion 2 IC, battalion second in command.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: That's right. He was also the deputy for Colonel Bob Stewart. But he reached the rank of colonel himself, ultimately; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so. I left the army in 1998, and what their actual ranks are now I'm not sure of.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have on e-court document 3D 00461.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: To save time, Mr. Williams, I'm going to read out two excerpts from the document that we will be seeing shortly on our screens. It is Colonel Brian Watters' letter that he wrote to his father from Bosnia-Herzegovina. His father was also a soldier, and he was trying to inform him and describe the situation to him. The exhibit was introduced in the Kordic/Cerkez case. It was D57/1. That was the exhibit number. I'm going to have it tendered here as well. I'll read it in the original, in English. I apologise for my pronunciation. But I'm going to read two excerpts. The first is at the very beginning. Have you got the document on your screen? Yes, we have, actually. One is the third paragraph marked by the side. He says the following: "It is all too easy [In English] to apportion blame to a specific faction prosecuting its particular military or political advantage. It is convenient to identify the culprit and level the blame in his direction. It is comfortable but too simplistic. There are no 'good guys and bad guys' in this bitter civil war, there are only victims." [Interpretation] And then later on in the letter, on page 3, the first paragraph, the whole first paragraph, or rather, there's a big paragraph to begin that says -- paragraph 2, beginning "Tonight, I deployed ..." The second sentence: [In English] There is a dispute between the Croats and Muslims over the positioning of their respective flags. Two Muslims were shot dead last night and one Croat earlier this evening. Those are, of course, allies, but then again this is Bosnia." [Interpretation] You were there for six months. You saw everything going on there; you experienced the general atmosphere and mood. Would you agree with these assessments made by Colonel Brian Watters?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would. Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd now like to move on to another area. Yesterday, and in your previous statement to the investigators, especially the 1995 one, you said, in a way - and it was on page 3315 of the transcript and page 37 of your testimony yesterday - you said that you believed that two incidents caused greater tension among the two parties, the two sides, which later resulted, in a way, in a direct conflict in Gornji Vakuf between the HVO and the army, BH army. And these two incidents, you say, were as follows: The first incident was the one in which the HVO soldier decapitated a retarded Muslim invalid. We just mentioned that a while ago today. And then the other one you mentioned was when HOS took over the school and threw out the Muslims. I have to say here that yesterday, in your testimony before the Court, you said that the HVO took over the school, whereas in your previous statement, paragraph 19 of the 2005 statement, you said that HOS took over the school. Let's clear that point up. What is it, HOS or the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The school did have HOS in it, and eventually it became used by the HVO. As to which one took it off the Muslim -- stopped the Muslims using it as well, I cannot answer definitely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, but we agree that HOS took over the school first and then later on, the HVO. One of the two expelled the Muslims from the school. But at any rate, you did mention that particular incident, when HOS took over the school, and the incident where the man's head was cut off, as events which, without a doubt, caused increased tension. Is that correct? Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were two of the incidents that helped to cause the problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, two days into your testimony, and in the proofing session with the Prosecutor on Sunday, when you go back to think about those days, would you say that that was the right description of events, that that was how things were?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were other incidents as well; some that we were aware of; others that we weren't aware of. But it was just a general increasing of tension and distrust.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, let's take a look at what others think about that, some of your colleagues, too. You said that Company B Major Alastair Rule was one of your superiors and he was your commander; right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: He testified before this Tribunal in the Kordic/Cerkez trial, and you testified there as well as a witness. Alastair Rule said on that occasion that the conflict in Gornji Vakuf came about when a bomb that had been planted exploded in the headquarters of the BH army, in a hotel in Gornji Vakuf. That is in the Kordic judgement. For the record, that's where it's to be found. Paragraph 561. For the benefit of the record and the Trial Chamber, I'd like to read the sentence. Major Rule gave evidence about the conflict, which was the start of the fighting in Central Bosnia. He said: "[In English] The fighting broke out in Gornji Vakuf on 11 January sparked by a bomb which had been placed in a Muslim-owned hotel used as a headquarters." [Interpretation] Do you agree with your commander's opinion?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. That was one of the pivotal events that actually started the actual conflict itself. The other incidents I referred to were helping to increase the tension.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Okay. The Cheshire Regiment commander while you were in Bosnia was Colonel Robert Stewart; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bob Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Bob Stewart, he was referred to.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You hold him in high esteem. I think he was a popular man, was he not, Bob Stewart? You were shaking your head, but for the record, could you give us an audible answer, please.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a very, very popular commander with the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Colonel Bob Stewart, in his book -- after serving in Bosnia, he published a book, which was very popular, I might add. It's called "Broken Lives," the title of the book. And on page 205 of that book --.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I'd like to ask the registrar to place it on e-court. It is 3D 00462. They are two pages. The first page just shows the title page and the second page is where the sentence is to be located.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: On page 205, Bob Stewart says that the conflict arose in Gornji Vakuf spontaneously, broke out spontaneously. Let me read the sentence. It's been underlined. May we pan down a bit. Thank you. "[In English] This flare-up just happened spontaneously, and we never discovered its cause," [Interpretation] says Bob Stewart. Did you hear Bob Stewart make that assessment earlier?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [In English] Okay. [Interpretation] Bob Stewart, when, later on, he testified in the Kordic-Cerkez trial, during the cross-examination, on page 12364 of the transcript, said as follows -- he says the following -- I won't read the question. The answer is this: "[In English] Well, I'll just actually qualify that given a second to think about it. Maybe it was the Vance-Owen Plan that was the catalyst for this fighting. I think I have actually said that somewhere. Actually, in rethinking it through, the answer to your question was, No, I don't know. But maybe it was this silly plan." [Interpretation] So from the quotation in the book and what he said before this Tribunal, we heard what he thinks about the causes of the conflict, what Bob Stewart thinks about the causes of the conflict. Did you hear of this position of his ever?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: About the Vance-Owen Peace Plan, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let's move on. The judgement in Kordic, paragraph 559, also quotes General Simpson, the high-ranking officer of the British Army, who, in the judgement and according to the judgement, said the following: "After the Vance-Owen Peace Plan was made public, the situation culminated, especially in Gornji Vakuf and in the Lasva River Valley. An all-out conflict broke out between the HVO and the ABiH." Do you agree with that assessment? Mr. Cordy-Simpson or General Cordy-Simpson also says that the conflict broke out as a result of the Vance-Owen Plan. Would you agree with that? Say you do or you don't or you don't know.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do agree with the general's assessment that the Vance-Owen Peace Plan was the culminating point. There were put -- it was just part of other incidents that were just creating more and more mistrust between the two sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to quote another opinion, and it is, once again, in the Kordic judgement, paragraph 564, which quotes a witness and he is Brigadier -- HVO Brigadier Luka Sekerija is his name, and the judgement quotes that the conflict broke out with an all-out attack by the BH army against HVO positions on the 11th of January, 1993. And after that, Luka Sekerija states - and this is interpreted in that paragraph 564 - that after the war, officers of the BH army told him that they had received an order to expel the Croats from Gornji Vakuf, first of all, in October, 1992, and he says that on page 18154 of the transcript, and then again in January, 1993, because they considered that area to be the front door entrance into Central Bosnia. That's what is said in the judgement, and Sekerija said that on page 18222 of the transcript. So, according to that witness quoted in the judgement, it is the strategical value or position of Gornji Vakuf that is referred to. Do you agree? And I think, judging by what you said a moment ago, that you would agree, that it was of strategic importance for both armies, that Gornji Vakuf was the key strategic point and therefore the key reason for the conflict. Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was the fact that it straddled the routes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Next we have another interesting document, and it is a report by the ECMM, the European Monitoring Mission, of the 19th of January.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have it on our screens, please. The document is P 01215. And I have to say the judgement in the Kordic trial, in the same paragraph, 564 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Is that under seal?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, none of this is under seal. Thank you. Thank you for your concern. I do apologise. I'm not sure about P 1215, but it's quoted. It's quoted in the Kordic judgement but only by date. So just to be on the safe side, I'll ask for us to go into private session, because most of these documents were, indeed, under seal. Perhaps this one is not, but unfortunately I failed to check.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, please, can we move into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we look at the last page of this document, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in open session, Your Honour. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir. My name is Slobodan Praljak. I am an accused. I will put some brief questions to you, and I see that your responses are brief, so we will get through them the material, I hope. Do you know how many soldiers of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina defended Jajce together with the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I'm aware, it was a brigade of each. It happened -- it fell before we actually deployed, so it was something that had already happened before we got there.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Well, we shall see that the Jajce brigade of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina arrived in the Gornji Vakuf area. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: You said twice that that brigade, or rather, the men in that brigade numbered 50. Can you testify that a brigade, defending Jajce, stationed in Gornji Vakuf, numbered only 50 men? And in what army can 50 men be called a brigade?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was the part of the escort when the Jajce Brigade that were in the Gornji Vakuf area were placed on coaches and taken out of the area, and they numbered approximately 50 men, some families. And the whole lot went into two coaches and a truck. There were no other Jajce Brigade soldiers that we were asked to escort out of the area. And they came from the villages of Voljevac, that area.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: So you are testifying that, after the conflict in Gornji Vakuf, the Jajce Brigade, by agreement, had to leave that area, and you saw that 50 men left.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. That was the only group of Jajce Brigade soldiers that we in B Company escorted out of the area.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. But from that one cannot conclude that what you saw were all the soldiers of the Jajce Brigade who had been stationed in Gornji Vakuf; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. But during the cease-fire negotiations, we were asked to escort them out, and that was the only group that we escorted out. If there were others, we had no knowledge of them. And nobody asked us to escort them out.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'm satisfied with that reply. What code designation did the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina carry, the one that arrived in Gornji Vakuf, after Jajce? What was their code designation?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall. It would either -- I think, have been either the 304th or the 317th, I think.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: The reason I'm asking you, sir, is that your recollection around the Tomislav Brigade, the Livno Brigade, the soldiers from Croatia, the hospital, and so on and so forth, are very precise and very clear. As an intelligence officer on the ground, you cannot tell me what code destination the brigade from Bosnia-Herzegovina carried which arrived in Gornji Vakuf? The answer is 305. What was the code destination of the ABiH brigade from Gornji Vakuf, the local brigade?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I would refer back to the question earlier. I can't quite remember. But I think it may have been either the 304th or the 317th. But it definitely began with a 3.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Could we see 3D 00456, please. While we will are waiting for the document to show up -- you can zoom in. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Please take a look at the document. You see here Gornji Vakuf, Bugojno, Novi Travnik, Travnik, and Jajce. My question is the following: When did the Serbs take Donji Vakuf; do you know?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, it was taken sometime around the fall of Jajce, but I'm not particularly certain on that. I know the front line in that area was fairly static because I went up to it quite a few times. But when it actually was taken I cannot say for definite.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Witness, I must interrupt you. Please excuse me. My questions are very simple, so in order to save time, and for that reason alone because I do not wish to be impertinent, please sell me precisely: Do you know when the Serbs took Donji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. As this happened in April, 1992, was all communication between Bugojno and Jajce, Bugojno-Donji Vakuf-Jajce cut off? And I mean all communication.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That I couldn't answer. Do you mean -- by "communication," do you mean roads or do you mean telephones or radios or ...

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Roads, I'm referring to roads. So neither BritBat nor convoys nor anyone could pass through. All road traffic towards Zenica, Tuzla, Travnik went along two routes: Gornji Vakuf-Novi Travnik and the second one was Gornji Vakuf-Bugojno-Novi Travnik. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was at that time, yes. But by the time we got there, there was just the route through Gornji Vakuf to Novi Travnik.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: So we can conclude that the fall of Jajce, you will agree with me, as regards road communications, had no relevance as regards communications or roads between Gornji Vakuf, Travnik, Tuzla, Zenica, Visoko, and so on; is that correct? Because it was cut off to the left of Travnik, in the direction of Jajce.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: When Jajce fell and the front line moved forward, it meant that the Serb artillery could move forward, and our commander's, Colonel Stewart's primary worry was that the Serb artillery, which was up on the hill overlooking Travnik and Turbe --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Yes. That is something we could talk about, but it wasn't my question. How many refugees arrived from Donji Vakuf to Gornji Vakuf, after the fall of Donji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That, I couldn't tell you now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know how many soldiers of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina from Donji Vakuf were stationed in Gornji Vakuf after the Serbs took Donji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This particular -- now I can't, no. I would have been able to years ago.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: If, in Gornji Vakuf, according to the census of 1991, there were 8.600 Croats and 10.480 Muslims, if we add to that the refugees from Jajce and the refugees from Donji Vakuf, how do you explain your claim that in the conflict in January, 1993, the HVO was superior in numbers?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the HVO brought up the reinforced brigades, they outnumbered, and they also had the heavy weaponry which the armija did not have. They had more -- they had tanks, artillery, heavy mortars. The armija had very few things like -- battle-winning assets like that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Let's leave weapons to one side now. Sir, Witness, we're not talking about artillery and mortars but manpower, and you have answered. My next question: How long was the front line on the Livno theatre towards the Serbs and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak has just addressed an issue relating to refugees. I see he has quoted, line 18, page 85. So this was a census of 1991. In Gornji Vakuf there were 8.600 Croats and 10.480 Muslims. According to you, do these figures represent the town or the entire municipality? Because in the indictment, in 1971 [as interpreted], the town had 10.000 inhabitants, 5.000 of which were located in Gornji Vakuf. So what about the town of Gornji Vakuf? According to you, how many inhabitants were there in Gornji Vakuf itself? I'm not talking about the entire municipality here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember, Your Honour, so I cannot give a definite answer on that, other than the population had expanded with the influx of refugees, the vast majority of which were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but you were there. You were in Gornji Vakuf. According to you, this town had a thousand, 5.000, 10.000, 20.000 inhabitants? Do you have an idea? I'm just talking about the town itself.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I no longer have an idea of the number, Your Honour. It was only a small town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Praljak, proceed. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Sir, you're a soldier. Do you know how long the Livno-Tomislavgrad-Prozor front line was held by the brigades from Livno and Tomislavgrad against the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. These days I can't. I can show roughly where it is, where it was on a map.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Can you imagine a military situation where Colonel Siljeg would withdraw the brigades assigned to guarding or keeping a certain territory and send them to Vakuf? If he had brigades to spare, would it have been logical to send them to Gornji Vakuf? Or would the truth be that only small parts of those brigades were brought there?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I replied yesterday, there were two brigades, reinforced brigades, involved in the attack, and the reinforcements were sub-units that had come from other brigades.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: You will agree that we saw this in General Petkovic's order, where he sent 3 times 100 and 1 times 70 men. If 370 men arrived to replace people, can we agree that it was so, or was it something else?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That is a troop rotation. They were there to relieve other soldiers.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes, but 370. Sir, on the map before you, can you mark the line held against the Serbs? Where did it go? From Gornji Vakuf, where was the line against the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I recall, it's something like that. Maybe that bit is a bit further that way. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Could you please show the witness the map. Could you flip it down. Your Honours, this map is 1:50.000. I have an identical map but it's 1:25.000. So, if Your Honours wish to look, you may look at this map, for your information. The only difference is that the defence lines against the Serbs are not marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness -- Your Honours, before we are going to deal with this map, could Mr. Praljak tell us who made the markings on this specific map so that we have that on the record, and the source. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] The legend is already on the map, and it was General Petkovic and I who made the markings, based on documents, unfortunately in prison conditions, so it's not a professional job. But red marks the HVO positions, green marks the ABiH positions, and black marks the positions against the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Your Honours, sorry, I would like to interrupt again. If General Praljak says that this was based on documents, could he be a bit more specific? Which documents were actually used in order to prepare these markings on the map? We really need to know which specific documents General Praljak is referring to. And also the time period is important. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] The time period is just before the beginning of the conflict in Gornji Vakuf, and the documents are the Prosecution documents we have all seen here: Colonel Siljeg's reports, Mr. Cikotic's reports, and a gentleman I will quote soon, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Sorry, I think we need to be more specific. If it's just a report from Siljeg, could you please provide us with the exhibit numbers?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour. [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't think the accused is bound to say precisely on the basis of what documents. The witness can confirm or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you have a map, which is 1:25.000, in which General Praljak has positioned the HVO units in green and the ABiH units -- the HVO is in red and the ABiH is in green. In Gornji Vakuf, for instance, you can see that there were, all at once, the ABiH and the HVO. Now, in looking at this map, do you think this could match what you, yourself, noticed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is roughly how I recall it, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you don't challenge the markings on this map.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For instance, let's take Bistrica, which is above Gornji Vakuf. You can see that there are HVO positions there and a few ABiH positions. Would that be in line with the perception you had of the situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
